en: The seventh chapter:
For a hero who has made his vow, the earth is a stage for combat, the ocean is a mere canal, the netherworld is dry land, and Mount Sumeru is a mere anthill. (7.1)
That the mountains do not bow before this mighty-armed one who holds his bow is indeed a marvel;
what need is there even to mention those wretched crows known as enemies?
Then, after some days had passed, on a most auspicious day calculated by hundreds of astrologers,

at a moment for military expedition (*daṇḍayātrā*) deemed suitable for victory in all four directions, he bathed with jars of refined gold and polished silver— resembling autumnal clouds skilled in releasing water— and performed worship to the Blessed One with supreme devotion.
Having offered oblations into the fire—whose flames blazed upward and whose mass of crests turned to the right—to the deity Nīlalohita;

having given to the twice-born thousands of silver and gold vessels filled with sesame seeds adorned with jeweled ornaments, and tens of millions of cows whose hooves and horn-tips were decorated with creepers of golden leaves; and having sat upon an auspicious throne spread with a tiger skin, he first smeared his body, beginning from the feet, with sandalwood paste as white as his own fame, after first anointing his weapons.
Having put on a pair of fine silk garments resembling the markings of a royal swan couple,
having placed upon his head a wreath of white flowers and jasmine buds as the sign of the Supreme Lord— like a crescent moon—
and having brought to the range of his ears a fresh sprout of dūrvā grass smeared with yellow orpiment, like the emerald rays of an ear-ornament;
Having fastened upon his forearm the *pratisara*—an amulet for the auspiciousness of the journey—along with the circle of royal edicts;

having had his head sprinkled by a profusion of droplets of peace-water scattered from the hands of the highly honored and delighted domestic priest; and having dispatched costly vehicles while distributing among the kings ornaments that illuminated the quarters with the luster of abundant gems.
Having liberated the world of afflicted and wretched sons of noble family through gifts bestowed with grace and having released all their bonds, he—

his own self as it were proclaimed by the radiance of that moment’s remembrance— appointed his right pillar-like arm to the office of conquering the eighteen islands amidst a competitive scramble, while all his attendants, as if possessed of supernatural signs, stood before him like servants.
Amidst a tumultuous roar of shouts of victory being raised by the delighted subjects, he emerged from his palace like Hiraṇyagarbha emerging from the cosmic egg to inaugurate the Kṛta Yuga;
and not far from the city, on the banks of the Sarasvatī, he went to a great structure made of grass that had been constructed,
where lofty archways were erected.
Upon which golden jars were placed as ornaments with sprouts arranged upon the altar, where garlands of forest flowers were bound,
and which was graced by white banners;
While a Brahmin was reciting in a temple where white-robed attendants were wandering about, he set out;

and as he stood there, the village accountant, accompanied by his entire staff of officials, said: "May Your Majesty, whose commands are never in vain, perform the taking of the day's census this very day."
Having said, "Of the teachings," he presented a seal made of gold, bearing the emblem of the bull and newly fashioned.
The king took it;
but as soon as the first lump of clay had been placed before him, the seal slipped from his lotus-like hand and fell face-down upon the ground.
Upon the banks of the Sarasvatī, where the mud was soft and the layers of silt were only slightly dried, streaks of various colors shone forth with great clarity.
As his attendants grew despondent, fearing some ill omen, the king reflected thus in his mind: "The intellects of the undiscerning are indeed incapable of perceiving reality.
For instance, even when it has been indicated by an omen that the earth shall become marked by the seal of your sole sovereignty, common folk interpret it otherwise."

Having thus rejoiced in his mind at that great omen, he bestowed upon the twice-born a hundred villages whose boundaries were measured by a thousand ploughs. He spent that day there, and when night had fallen, having honored all the assembled kings, he went to sleep.
Then, as the third watch was passing away, while all living beings slept in silence and the deep roar of the world-elephants yawning in every direction resounded, the drum of departure was struck.
Having stood before it for a moment, eight sharp strokes were again clearly sounded on the drum to mark the number of *krośas* of the march.
Then, as the third watch was passing away, while all living beings slept in silence and the deep roar of the world-elephants yawning in every direction resounded, the drum of departure was struck.
The drum of departure stood before him for a moment, and then eight sharp strokes were clearly struck upon the drum to count the stages of the journey;
thereafter, as the drum resounded,
Where the *nāndī* drums resounded with joy, the *guñjā* berries hummed, and the *kāhala* trumpets blared;
While the conchs were sounding,
the clamor of the bracelets was gradually increasing,
and the attendants were occupied with the business of rousing [the king].
In the quarters resounded by the clamor of the pins and wedges being struck with swift blows from hammers;
while the multitudes of *pāṭīpati* officers were being bound by the military authorities;
and while the darkness of the night was being dispelled by the light of thousands of torches kindled by the people.
In the watchmen’s quarters, amorous couples were being roused from sleep by the movement of the feet of the female gatekeepers;

those who had fallen asleep were waking up and sitting up as they were driven away by harsh and bitter commands; and the bedchambers for the elephant-keepers were being vacated by the awakened herdsmen.
The horses, rising from sleep, shook their manes; the camp resounded with the noise of pickaxes digging the earth;
the clanging of hammers striking stakes echoed;
and the hooves of the horses galloped in waves, their rhythmic stamping amplified by the loud jingling of the fetters being fastened.
The ten directions were filled to overflowing with the clanging sound of iron chains being struck as they were fastened to rutting elephants;
the elephant’s hide was being wiped clean and flapped about on the elephant’s back, which had been scrubbed until it was free of dust by blows from bundles of straw;
and the canvas tents, awnings, curtains, and canopies were being wrapped and draped by the household servants.
In which the flattened leather bags were being filled with bundles of stakes;
where the storekeepers were busily packing their goods; and where many pack-horses were being driven along by attendants to transport the contents of the storehouse.
In that place, the houses of the feudatories were crowded with heaps of treasure-jars being placed upon motionless elephants by Niṣāda women;
wicked elephants were being loaded with collections of equipment hurled swiftly by clever Dāseraka servants stationed at a distance;
and there arose laughter among the people from the sight of pot-bellied *cuṇḍī* women, who were dependent on others and dragged along with difficulty as their buttocks leaned sideways.
In which the great, intoxicated elephants were rendered motionless as their bodies were constrained by the straps of excellent leather thongs pressed against them;
in which a fever was produced in the ears by the *ṭāṅkāra* clanging of bells attached to the herds of elephants;
and in which young camels were made to cry out, distressed by the neck-rings being fastened upon their backs.
In which noble sons of kings were being dispatched with loads of base metals; where the wives of well-born and respectable families were being conveyed in vehicles crowded with goods;

where elephant-drivers, deceived at the hour of departure, were searching for new attendants; and where the king’s favorite war-horses were being led away by foot-soldiers carrying gifts of royal favor.
In which the grandeur of the circles of the vanguard was established by handsome and skillful soldiers;
where the *talasāraka* drums were joined together, equipped with rows of small bells made of salted peas being measured out by the station-keepers;
and where the monkeys were being placed upon the branches by the troop-leaders of the beloved horses, who were themselves entangled in nets of protective cords coiled into rings.
In which the sprouts of the morning fodder were being pulled by the grooms,

while the shouts of the grass-cutters were spreading with loud cries; and where a great commotion was occurring in many stables caused by young horses with upturned muzzles rearing and stumbling due to the haste of their departure.
While beautiful women, hastening at the call of their riders, were applying facial ointments to those mounted on caparisoned female elephants;
while stores of fodder and grain were being plundered by common neighbors running after the moving elephants and horses; and while wagons were being overwhelmed by wandering herds of oxen.
On the road where the tracks were struck by the multitude of carts creaking as their wheels turned, where oxen laden with sudden loads of goods leaped up unexpectedly,
and where the first bulls of the *saurabheya* breed hung low and stretched forward, greedy for the fodder nearby;
In which the great kitchens of the chief ministers were being set in motion;
where flag-bearers ran ahead;
and where the exit from the narrow interior of the huts was found with difficulty by hundreds of loved ones.
While the nearby witnesses were being struck with clods of earth by the people rising from the huts trampled by the feet of elephants,

while the small families of the tiger-settlements were fleeing amidst the jostling and collisions, and while the merchants were despondent as their draft-oxen bolted away, harassed by the clamor and the plundering of their wealth;
The inner apartments were departing with a multitude of female elephants whose crowds of followers were thinning out under the light of the torches carried before them;
dogs were being called out by the horsemen;
and the quality of the lofty ramparts was being praised as "khakkhaṭa" (firm), for it provided the pleasure of a steady gait due to the forceful stamping of their feet.
At the time of his departure, when the world was devoured by the king and the southern cavalrymen were sinking in despair,
betrayed by their faltering horses, there arrived from every direction elephant-drivers mounted upon female elephants, holding aloft bows variegated with patterns of gold-leaf.

There were those seated on intermediate thrones with close attendants holding swords; those with betel-bearers waving chowrie-palmettoes; and those at the rear seats with quivers, ornaments, slings, and bundles of arrows placed beside them.
With saddle-cloths made to look like budding sprouts by means of curved golden rods shaped like leafy creepers;
with their steady placement ensured by silk pillows fixed in position by the binding straps of the saddle-flaps;
and with the sounds of jeweled stone-plates on their hooves resonating as they struck against the jingling iron-shoes.
They were adorned with garments whose lower legs were concealed by delicate, variegated eye-patterns; with reddish-brown robes stained with saffron dye that turned them a mottled tawny hue;
with white bodies shining with dark-blue *rājāvarta* patterns produced by the contrast of smooth, bee-black woolen cloths joined with white silk;
and with tunics, fine Chinese shirts, and quilted coats (*vārabāṇa*) fringed with clusters of large pearls, as well as turbans variegated with various dyed silks.

They were adorned with turbans that eclipsed the luster of a parrot’s plumage; they carried beautiful weapons tucked into their sides after strenuous exercise; their attendants ran about to untangle the curling locks of hair falling from necklaces that swayed with their movements; their earrings jingled as they brushed against ear-ornaments of golden leaf-sprouts; the stalks of their ear-lotuses were held fast by the folds of their turbans;

their heads were veiled by delicate saffron-dyed upper garments; they wore linen tunics inlaid with fragments of crest-jewels; and the swarms of bees upon their crests acted like peacock-feather parasols.
There were staffs for driving the *śārika* and *śārivāha* birds encountered on the road;
furthermore, the world’s interior was filled with fierce and agile warriors leaping about, adorned with circles of shimmering yak-tail whisks (*cāmara*) and variegated *kārdaraṅga* skins;

the quarters of the sky were made resonant by the tinkling of golden ornaments on hundreds of charging Kamboja horses; and the cavities of the ears were deafened by the sharp sound of hundreds of *lambā* drums beaten mercilessly.
The palace gate was filled with kings whose names were being proclaimed aloud, and who waited for the delivery of commands with their faces upturned toward the foot-soldiers.
And when the blessed Maker of Day had risen, the signal conch resounded repeatedly, announcing the time for the king to enter the assembly hall.

Then, not long after his first departure for the conquest of the quarters, he was carried by a female elephant named Siddhayātrā, who seemed to summon the world-elephants (diggajas) with the playful swaying of her ears tossed in her movement;

while a ceremonial umbrella was held over him— a magnificent umbrella with a handle of cat’s-eye gem, its surface reddened as if out of anger at the sight of the rising sun because it was inlaid with fragments of ruby whose rays shimmered upon it, and which possessed a softness exceeding the core of a plantain tree, as if it were fashioned from fresh lotus fibers.
Like a second lord of serpents with his body encased in a garment, he was like the day of the churning of the ocean, wearing robes as white as a mass of foam from the Sea of Milk;
though still a youth, he had ascended the throne of Indra like a young *pārijāta* tree.

With the pollen from the clusters of flowers in his ear-ornaments—shaken by the wind of the waving fly-whisks—he seemed to smear the quarters of the sky with a powder for subjugating the entire world, while the rising sun’s reflection appeared reddish-pink upon the crest-jewel set before him.
As if drinking even the sun with his splendor, he seemed to bestow other continents through his lip-line smeared with thick betel and vermilion;
making even the quarters of the sky grasp fly-whisks, as it were, in the form of the circles of rays from his shimmering great pearl necklace;
and with his creeper-like brow, which was raised by three parts by the glances of the assembly of kings, he seemed to command even the three worlds to pay tribute.

As if enclosing with his exceedingly long arm-like ramparts all seven great ocean-trenches out of a desire for protection; embraced by Fortune who had emerged after taking away the entire sweetness of the Ocean of Milk;

appearing as if intensely composed of nectar while being drunk in by the thousands of eyes of the courtly folk upturned in curiosity; and sinking, as it were, through the weight of his virtues into the hearts of kings moistened with affection.
Anointing the beholders with the liquid of his own good fortune—like the Lord of the Immortals, anxious to wash away the stain of the fratricide;
like Pṛthu, clearing away all the kings of the earth through his intent upon purifying the world;

preceded by thousands of light-bringing attendants who, like the rays of the sun, were restless in their skill at office yet stern in establishing order, and who were separated from the crowds of people fleeing in fear—[he advanced].
As if making the ten directions their own,
as if establishing even the wind— in whose movement they had swallowed up the falling swaying plantain trees— in the path of discipline,
and as if driving away even the rays of the sun, which were shaken by the mass of dust raised by their swift feet;
The king went forth, driving the crowds of people here and there with staff-bearers who, as if by the light of their golden cane-staves, seemed to cast away even the day itself;
and he bowed down, his body bent in humility.

While the circle of kings stood with hearts trembling with fear, their heads beautiful with the mass of rays from their crowns of gems and gold loosened by their agitation, and the dust from their flower-crests scattered about;
The rays of the crest-jewels of the luminous ones—darting downward, sideways, and upward—set forth like other intentions for the sake of securing auspicious omens.

Thick with dust that acted like clouds, garlands of tender sprouts from the wish-fulfilling trees rose up into the sky like peacocks; and these were fastened as if they were plumage by the world-protectors at the gates of the quarters.
And he was being saluted by the guardians of the directions with various glances of the eyes, side-long looks, full gazes, arched eyebrows, and half-smiles.

With jests, clever conversation, inquiries after welfare, reciprocal salutations, and the wild glances of his eyebrows, as well as by issuing commands, the hero distributed among the princes— as was fitting for each— his own life-force consisting of pride, as if purchasing it with gifts of affection.

Then, as the king set forth, the exceedingly loud resonance of musical instruments spread across the horizons, like the trumpeting of world-elephants terrified by a great clamor echoing here and there.

From the world-elephants (*diggaja*), the rut-fluids of the elephants in their fury flowed forth in three streams; with these paths of ichor, dark as swarms of bees, thousands of tributary rivers of the Yamunā seemed to flow.
As the sun’s orb turned crimson with masses of vermilion dust, the birds suspected it was the hour of sunset.
The sounds of kettledrums were drowned out by the trumpeting of the elephants’ ears, which was rich with the humming of bees.
The multitude of chowries, being violently shaken, swept across the entire universe with all its moving and unmoving beings.
The sky was rendered continuous by masses of foam—white as garlands of Sindhuvara flowers—cast up from the mouths of the horses in the cavalry.
Forests of umbrellas with handles of refined gold, pale as clusters of gathered Tagara blossoms, seemed to drink in the day as they struck one another, causing the eight directions to vanish.
The day, obscured by the dust of the armies, shone forth through the morning sunlight from the rows of gems upon the crowns;
and the quarters of the sky, rendered deaf by the echoing clamor of silver ornaments and golden trappings that resounded, became as if made of lapis lazuli.
The elephants sprinkled the circle of the directions with droplets from their rutting heat, as if to extinguish the fire of the enemy’s prowess.
The flickering rays of their crest-jewels robbed his eyes of the power to open;
the king himself was struck with wonder as he cast his gaze in every direction and beheld his army departing from its quarters of residence,
like the world of living beings emerging from the belly of Adhokṣaja at the beginning of a cosmic age.

Like the ocean rising from the mouth of Agastya, flooding the world; like the current of the Narmadā flowing forth in a thousand streams after being compressed and released by the thousand staff-like arms of Arjuna:
"Flow forth, my son!"
"Friend, why do you delay?
The horse is leaping!
Good sir, you move as if your feet were broken, while these attendants ahead are falling upon us with great impetuosity."
Why do you drive the camel? Do you not see, O merciless one, the young child lying there, devoid of all feeling?
Child Rāmila, stay close by so that you do not get lost in the dust; do you not see how the bag of barley flour is spilling?
Why are you thus hurrying in such haste? O bull, why do you abandon your path and run into the midst of the horses?
O fisherwoman, you enter the path of the Mātaṅgas, O mother, desiring to go there.
My dear, the sack of chickpeas is leaking sideways;
do you not heed me as I cry out?
You are descending toward the edge of the pit!
"Stay at ease, you wanton woman! Sauvīraka, the jar is broken!
Mantharaka, you will eat sugar-cane once it has been carried away!"
"Satisfy the bull!
Servant, how much longer will you gather jujube fruits?
There is a long way to go."
Why do you flee this very day, Droṇaka?
The punitive expedition is long; there is no way for us to escape except by means of Niṣṭhuraka alone.
"Staphuṭaka, Sthāvara, clear the path ahead so that you do not break the vessel of molasses."
"A load of *gaṇḍaka* rice is too heavy for this young ox to carry.
Dāsaka, quickly cut a mouthful of fodder from these beans with a sickle;
who knows what will become of him once he has gone into the pasture?"
Dhava, drive back the oxen;
this field is protected by the Vāhīkas. The cart has become stuck.
Yakṣapālita, yoke a white bull capable of bearing the burden to the pole;
you are crushing these women!
"Why are your eyes bulging? You wretched elephant-driver,
you are stumbling in the mud of the trampling crush, while the trunk-staff of the elephant is close at hand!"
O brother, friend bereft of affection,
lift this ox from the mud!
Come here, young man!
"In this narrow passage crowded by the collision of dense herds of elephants, there is no way to escape"—

with such various conversations proceeding, [the caravan] was being cheered by a circle of bold men consisting of jesters, guards, fat merchants, porters, messengers, robbers, servants, cheats, and outcastes, who were shouting "kilakila" with playful clamor, nourished by the remnants of abundant crops crushed at their will and satisfied by the leftovers of their meals.

Accompanied by fellow villagers who, having acquired miserable hamlets through their afflictions, had gathered together out of the exhaustion and agitation caused by the toil of transporting the meager provisions of their withered cattle, and who themselves had taken up household utensils, they said:
"Let this single expedition of punishment somehow proceed;
let greed go to the depths of Pātāla, for it is the source of misfortune."
"May it be well!
Let him perform service!
May there be prosperity for this camp, which is a mass of all sufferings!"—thus was he being reviled by impoverished, elderly sons of noble families.

In some places, the procession moved with extreme speed, crowded by people who seemed as if they were woven together or bound in rows by being swept along in the current of an exceedingly sharp torrent;

it was filled with royal servants and porters carrying kitchen utensils, who— bearing heavy clubs on their dark and sturdy shoulders and clutching golden footstools, water-pots, ewers, and spittoons in their hands— were irresistible in their pride of seizing the royal requisites as they approached, and who were making everyone else move out of the way.

He pushed aside the people before him with those carrying loads of baskets crowded with copper cooking-pots, cauldrons, ladles, and vessels; who were matted with clusters of hanging monkeys, partridges, and sparrows bound by leather straps; who were gathering young hares, leaves of herbs, and tips of canes; whose faces were partially covered with white cloths to protect the fresh seals on their secret containers of milk products; and who were bearing burdens of heavy boxes and pans.

In some places, the world of noble sons was being distressed by wicked servants appointed to guide weak oxen that stumbled at every step, while the oxen themselves cried out, "The distress is ours; at the time of the harvest, other scoundrels will come forward!
Elsewhere, the countryside folk were running and rushing on both sides out of curiosity to see the king.

The road was crowded with village headmen and petty officials emerging from the countryside, who had halted their progress at the front by supporting water-jars with their aged elders; they carried baskets of curds, molasses, sugar-candy, and flowers as offerings, and moved forward in hurried groups.

Terrified by the intimidation of fierce and angry police officers, they fled great distances, yet stumbled, fell, and kept their eyes fixed upon the king, even as they denounced the faults of former governors—though these were non-existent—to hundreds of newly appointed officials.

And [the road] was filled with clouds of dust being raised by those praising [the king] and recounting his long-standing favors; in some places, it was being trampled by circles of cavalrymen moving in secret, while the protection of the crops sought after by the Gauḍas was being maintained;
and by others, who were delighted by the guards assigned to them, who uttered praises such as "Dharma is a visible god" in loud voices.

Others, their despair made manifest by the crops that were being reaped and brought to completion, had departed from their fields with their entire families out of grief; with their very life-breaths already severed, they were stripped of all fear by their intense anguish, crying out: "Where is the king?
From where has the king come?
And what kind of king is he?"
Thus began the mockery of the king;
meanwhile, some hares, pursued at every step by packs of swift and fierce staff-bearers and struck here and there like mountain-balls,

moved about, while others, seized by the great crowd that had descended all at once, were being torn to pieces like sesame seeds, though they were skilled in escaping through the gaps between the shanks of many creatures.

It was filled with the forced clamor of those escaping from their lives by means of many horses thrown off by crooked maneuvers, and by falling clods of earth, clubs, arrows, axes, stakes, spades, hoes, sickles, staves, and showers of rain;
elsewhere, it was crowded with groups of fodder-carriers whose hips were covered by nets of fodder grey with the dust of chaff, and whose sickles dangled from parts of their old saddles.
The air was thick with clouds of dust raised by those being led along, who wore tattered, filthy, and loose blankets of coarse wool or ragged, patched rags granted as favors by their lords;
here and there, the future war with Gauḍa was being discussed in circles formed by groups of men moving toward a secluded spot.

In some places, the bundles of grass were being torn up by the entire populace, who were distracted by orders to fill the muddy patches; in other places, Brahmins were crying out in dispute from the tops of trees as they were being frightened away by the staff-bearers stationed there;
and in yet other places, village dogs were being dragged along by the villagers while being entangled in the snares of the hunters.
In some places it was adorned by the jostling of throngs of horses being ridden by princes eager to display their mutual prowess; through its manifold events, it generated wonder,
like the ocean of universal dissolution set upon swallowing the world.
It was as if created for the protection of great serpents like the netherworld (Pātāla),

or fashioned for the residence of the Supreme Lord like Mount Kailāsa; it was like a treasury of the four ages’ creation containing the succession of all living beings visible therein, and like the performance of asceticism by the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis)— though fraught with hardship— bringing about a series of auspicious results.

Beholding it thus, he proceeded toward the camp. And to those who were nearby, he said: "The roads for the conquest of the quarters were prepared by the venerable Māndhātṛ; yet by Raghu, with the irresistible speed of his chariot, the pacification of the directions was accomplished in a very short time."

With his bow as his only companion, Pāṇḍu, the son of Pāṇḍu—Savyasācin—brought under tribute those kings who were arrogant with the pride of their hereditary strength of arm, their noble lineage, and their wealth;

having crossed the land of the Jinas, he conquered Mount Hemakūṭa for the sake of the Rājasūya sacrifice—a mountain whose groves resounded with the twanging of the tips of the Gandharvas' bows as they grew enraged.
For the swift, victory is separated from them only by their own resolve.
Although separated by the Himavat and Mahāhimavat mountains, the tree-like Drumakīrti, trembling with fear at the encounter of arms, bore the hand of the Kaurava lord like a servant;

for the kings of old were indeed not overly desirous of conquest, since on such a small portion of the earth there were many monarchs, such as Bhagadatta, Dantavakra, Krātha, Karṇa, Śiśupāla, Sālva, Jarāsandha, and the King of Sindhu.
King Yudhiṣṭhira was contented, for he endured even the kingdom of the Kimpuruṣas, which caused the world to tremble at the victory of Dhanañjaya;
and Caṇḍakośa was indolent, for he did not enter the earth after conquering it, remaining instead in the kingdom of women.
For those possessed of energy, however, the distance between the Snowy Mountain and Mount Gandhamādana is indeed very short.
Kiṣku is the region of Turuṣka;
Prādeśa is the land of the Pārasīkas;
Śaśapada is the abode of the Śakas.
On the Pāriyātra mountain, where no obstacles are seen, the journey is easy;
the Deccan is easily accessible, having valor as its price.

Near the mountain Dardura, whose cave-dwellings are made beautiful by the fragrance of sandalwood creepers stirred by the breezes from the waves of the southern ocean, lies Malaya, and Mahendra is likewise attached to Malaya.

Hearing such conversations from the princes, who were strong-armed and indicative of their resolve, he reached his residence. At the palace gate, having been respectfully dismissed from the royal entourage by the two creeper-like hands [of the door-keeper], he entered and descended to a seat placed in the outer assembly pavilion. Having cast off all formalities, he sat for a moment.

Then, there the doorkeeper, placing his sprout-like hands upon the surface of the earth, announced: "Your Majesty, a messenger named Haṃsavega, sent by the Prince, the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, stands at the middle of the archway, desiring an audience.
The King, however, respectfully commanded: "Admit him immediately."
Then, due to his efficiency and the king’s high regard for him, the doorkeeper himself went forth.

Immediately after, Haṃsavega emerged, displaying humility through his very appearance; he was auspicious and noble in his expansive form, which brought joy to the eyes, and his great weight of virtues was being surpassed by the multitude of men carrying a vast array of gifts who followed behind him.
He entered the royal palace;
from a distance, his body touching the courtyard with its five limbs, he performed a prostration.

Summoned with great honor by the cry, "Come, come!", he stepped forward and, having approached, placed his forehead-mark upon the footstool and, with his hands resting on the king's back, bowed again.
He occupied a nearby spot indicated by the affectionate glance of the king.
Then the king, slightly inclining his body and moving aside the female fly-whisk bearer who stood between them, turned toward him and asked with courtesy: "Haṃsavega, is the illustrious prince well?"
He replied to him: "Today the King is well, since he asks with such words bathed in affection, moistened by the liquid of friendship, and full of respect.

Having paused for a moment, as it were, he spoke again to the clever man: "For Your Majesty, who is the vessel for the splendor and enjoyments of the four oceans, a fitting gift other than a single heart filled with true devotion is difficult to find in this world."
Nevertheless, our master, in order to ensure that this message was not left unfulfilled, has rendered this ancestral *vāruṇa* umbrella named Ābhoga meaningful by placing it in its proper setting.
Many wonders are seen here that dispel curiosity;
for instance, every day, for the sake of coolness, a single ray from the thousand rays of the moon enters into its shade.
Upon entering which, immediately after deep meditation, the sweet masters who teach the lute of the teeth drip forth clear streams of lunar light as much as desired from their jeweled rods;
and which favors with its shade that person—whether past or future—who has been or will become the lord of the four oceans, like Varuṇa himself, and not anyone else;
and which the seven-flamed fire does not consume.
The spotted-horse does not carry away [the dust], nor does the water moisten it, nor do the particles of soil soil it.
"Old age does not yet wither him.
May Your Majesty deign to favor him with a glance; he will listen with confidence even to my message.
Having spoken thus, he turned to his own man and said: "Arise!"
"Show it to the God," he said.
And immediately upon these words, the man rose and drew forth [the object] from its casing fashioned of washed silk.
As that exceedingly white splendor was being drawn out, Hara, as it were, laughed aloud with impetuosity.
It was as if the world had emerged from the netherworld by means of the circle of the hood-slates of the serpent Śeṣa;
it was as if the Milky Ocean had stood still, having become a wheel in the sky;
and it was as if a canopy of autumnal clouds had been fashioned in the courtyard of the firmament.
The sky was as if filled with a flock of swans— the celestial chariots of the gods— with their broad wings outspread, appearing like a weary rest;
it was as if people beheld the birth-day of the moon, charming with its orb of white radiance emerging from the eye of Atri, or witnessed the very moment of the rising of Nārāyaṇa’s navel-lotus,
and as if a satisfaction born from the sight of a moonlit night at twilight was bestowed upon their eyes.
It was as if the great circle of the Mandākinī’s sandy banks had been sprinkled with water within the belly of the vast sky;
it was as if the day had been transformed into a full-moon night;

and it was as if the pairs of cakravāka birds near the lotus ponds—whose minds were tormented by the doubt that the moon was rising—had slowly parted from one another, their beaks opening as they dropped the tips of lotus stalks they were gathering.
The circles of palace peacocks turned their faces away, their beaks silenced by cries of "kekā" that were stifled by the fear of autumnal clouds;
meanwhile, the clusters of night-lotuses were awakened, their broad petals opening wide with a clear, boisterous laughter of joy at the risen moon.

With a mind filled with wonder, the king, together with his court, gazed respectfully upon him—who was like the Tilaka ornament of the three worlds—with a vision that ascended along the path of his staff.
Like the childhood of Śvetadvīpa,
like an incarnate portion of the autumnal moon,
like the very heart of Dharma.
It was like the dwelling-place of the moon-world,
like the face of universal sovereignty white with the luster of ivory ornaments,
and like the circle of the horizon of heaven whitened by a network of pearls.
With a center as white as thick moonlight, it was like a lunar halo; with its whiteness mocking the splendor of the conch, it was like the motionless ear-ornament of Airāvata;
pale as a whirlpool of the white Gaṅgā, it was like the foot of Trivikrama, worthy of the salutation of the three worlds;
and it was encircled by rows of chowries made of lotus-fibers from Lake Mānasa, as if embraced by the crest-light rays of Varuṇa’s crown-jewel.
Its summit was graced by a swan with outspread wings, motionless as if longing to hear the sound of the anklets of the Fortune of a Universal Monarch above;

it shone brilliantly, held like a staff by Vāsuki, whose hood was folded like a lotus bud, who was as smooth to the touch, and who—though paralyzed by its sovereign power—was transformed into a pillar;
and by its whiteness, it seemed to wash the path of the stars clean.
With the vastness of its continuous flow, it seemed to clothe the day;
with its great height, it seemed to humble the heavens;
and it stood as if presiding over all auspicious things.
Like a white pavilion for the Goddess of Fortune, like a cluster of blossoms on the trunk of the world-tree,
like the central orb of the moonlight,
and like a pure smile of fame;
It was like a mass of foam from the waters of sword-blades,
like a canopy of fame for his possession of valor— a great umbrella, a marvel to the three worlds.
When that first gift had been seen by the king, the officials gradually displayed the remainder of the tribute as follows:
ornaments marked with the signs of having been worn by renowned monarchs such as Bhagadatta, which had turned the quarters of the sky red with the rays of their most precious gems.
He saw heaps of crest-jewels set in coral settings,

pearl necklaces that seemed like causes for the whiteness of the Ocean of Milk, and linen garments as bright as the rays of the autumn moon, capable of withstanding the test of purity, coiled up in bamboo baskets variegated with many colors.
He saw heaps of drinking vessels made of mother-of-pearl, conch, and coral, carved by skilled artisans;

collections of Kārdaraṅga skins, their luster protected by covers and adorned with elegant patterns of beautiful gold leaf and possessing most graceful borders; and strips of Jātī cloth, soft as birch bark and pleasant to the touch.
He saw collections of very soft, variegated cloth coverlets and pillows stuffed with *samūruka* wool;
cane seats with surfaces as tawny as the blossoms of the *priyaṅgu*; books containing elegant sayings bound with agallochum bark;
and fresh betel nuts hanging from their sprouts—possessing the hue of ripe *pāṭala* and *paṭola* fruits, green as young *hārīta* birds, and sweetened with milk.

And there were mango creepers and stars [of flowers], as well as thick bamboo tubes filled with black aloe-wood oil, their bodies encased in the leaf-sheaths of the brown *kāpotika* insects that resemble the cheeks of an angry monkey;
these tubes were secured by silk cords and contained black aloe-wood of a hue like crushed collyrium, which dispels great heat, along with *gośīrṣa* sandalwood.
And there were heaps of camphor as white and clear as fragments of ice-stone;
of musk-pouches; of *kakkola* sprouts matted with clusters of ripe fruit;
and of *lavaṅga* flower-bunches and *jātī* fruit-clusters.
There were overflowing jars emitting the fragrance of exceedingly sweet honey-liquors, heaps of white and black yak-tail fans,
and chests containing numerous painted picture-boards with hanging brushes and gourds;
and there were pairs of kinnaras, forest-dwellers, jīvañjīvakas, and water-nymphs, their necks bound by golden chains, who captivated the senses with their curiosity.
He beheld musk deer that perfumed the quarters with their fragrance;

yak-cows familiar with wandering about the precincts of his house; birds such as parrots and mynas whose tongues were eloquent in the recitation of many fine sayings, confined within cages of cane variegated with liquid gold; ruddy geese within coral cages; and water-elephants bristling with strings of pearls from their lofty frontal globes.
And there were ivory staffs and earrings.
But the king, his heart gladdened by the sight of the parasol, took it to mind as an auspicious omen for his first journey;
and being pleased, he spoke to Haṃsavega: "My good man!"

"It is no cause for wonder that this great sunshade—worthy of being borne upon the head of the Supreme Lord, the abode of all jewels—was obtained from Prince Kumāra, just as the moon is obtained from the great ocean.
Indeed, the childhood learning of the great serves as their benefactions.
Having removed that collection of gifts from that spot and having stood there for a moment, he said, "Haṃsavega!"
"Rest now," he said, and dismissed the chamberlain.

He himself also rose, bathed, and desiring auspiciousness, entered the shade of the Ābhoga mountain facing the east. Then, as he was entering, the moon's orb—seeming to be led to the state of a crest-jewel by the chill born of its shadow—was kissed, as it were, by water droplets that fell like rain.
Moonstones melted upon the slope of her forehead like camphor dust; pearl necklaces, turned into mist by the clusters of dripping dew-drops, were fastened around her neck like garlands;

a continuous stream fell upon her breast as if from the essence of yellow sandalwood; her heart became as cool as if made of white lotuses; and like a hidden slab of ice dissolving away, she anointed her limbs with extreme cold.
Filled with wonder, he thought to himself: "Aside from this one imperishable union, what other 'counter-reward' could there be?

And at the time of the meal, he gave to Hasavega a food-offering consisting of a washed coconut wrapped in a white cloth, containing the remains of sandalwood paste that had been smeared [upon him], as well as two garments touched by his own limbs—garments whose borders were adorned with clusters of pearls as bright as autumn stars.
He sent a waist-belt that turned the day red with the light of exceedingly precious ruby-jewels, an ear-ornament named Taraṅgaka, and an abundant variety of foods;
and in this manner, the day passed away.
Then the sun, its body greyed by the thick dust from the army stationed at Kaṭakasthala, descended into the western ocean as if to wash away its soiled limbs.

It departed for the quarter of Varuṇa to announce, as it were, the news of the granting of the vast royal umbrella. At that very moment, the earth, along with its islands, became like one who had joined her palms in salutation before the king, as all the groves of lotuses began to close their buds.
The crimson glow of twilight seized the world, as if it were the beautiful gesture of the joined palms of all living beings in homage to the king’s affection.
The eastern quarter turned dark, as if apprehensive of an offense committed against the Gaudas.
The earth, shrouded in a mass of accumulated darkness, spread a pallor of blackness, as if it were the extinguished embers of the fires of the majesty of other kings.
The clusters of stars scattered across the quarters of the sky, as beautiful as blooming *tagara* flowers, resembled a heap of blossoms strewn at the seat of the Lord of the Earth’s wrath.
A path of dust, pale as an elephant, shone in the firmament like the trail of Airāvata hastening toward the scent of rut from the fragrant elephants of the royal camp.
The Lover of Rohiṇī abandoned the vault of heaven and ascended to the sky, as if fleeing from the Pauruṣṭuti region after being pursued by the scent of the enraged tiger-king.
The moonbeams, piercing the hearts of proud women like news of an impending departure, spread through the ten directions;
the lords of the armies, their courage shaken as if terrified by the expedition of a new king, were thrown into agitation;
and the moonlight, having cast off the mass of darkness that obscured all hope, entered the hearts of the mountains like a thought entering the hollows of caves.
Sleep fled from the eyes of the rival kings, as it did from the beds of night-lotus groves.
At that hour, the king, reclining beneath a wide-spreading canopy, dismissed his attendants with the words, "Depart for now," and commanded Haṃsavega, "Relate your message.
Having bowed, he began to speak: "Your Majesty,..."
Long ago, from the Goddess Earth—who had conceived a fetus through contact with the Great Boar—was born a son named Naraka in the subterranean realm (Rasātala).
Even as a mere child, he became the crest-jewel of the World-Guardians, who were devoted to bowing at his feet.

And though the sun was gazed upon by the side-long glances of the female chakravaka bird in the lotus-pool of his palace—glances crooked with anger because he was a conqueror of the three worlds and arrogant in his arms—the sun did not go to its setting without his command, even as his chariot was turned back, trembling with fear and reddened by alarm.
And in the lineage of that great-souled one who snatched away this parasol— the very heart of Varuṇa manifest externally—

after many great kings as lofty as Mount Meru, such as Bhagadatta, Puṣpadatta, Vajradatta, and others, had passed away, there was born [the son] of Candramukhavarman, the grandson of the great king Mahārāja Bhūtivarman and the son of Pramottra.
To that god who dwells steadfastly on Kailāsa and whose armor is his stability, was born a great emperor named Susthiravarman,
a mass of splendor whom people called Mṛgāṅka;
he was born as if with egoism itself, like the elder brother Aja.
And he who, even as a boy, out of affection caused the twice-born to accept all manner of gifts and out of enmity the enemies;
and in whom resided that supreme sweetness of Fortune born from the ocean, which is otherwise so difficult to obtain;
and likewise, who seized the conch-shells of the lords of armies, but not their jewels.
He took the stability of the earth but not its tax; he assumed the dignity of the mountains but not their harshness.

And to that god whose name is auspiciously invoked, by his queen Śyāmādevī, was born a son named Bhāskaradyuti—also known as Bhāskaravarman—who, like the youth Bhīṣma, was begotten upon the daughter of the Ganges by Saṃtanu.

And this resolve of his, formed since childhood— that "I shall not bow to anyone other than the two lotus-feet of Śiva"— and such a desire, which is difficult to attain even in the three worlds, can be fulfilled by only one of three things:
either by the conquest of the entire world, or by death, or else by the conflagration of the quarters produced by the fire of a king’s fierce majesty.

"Friendship with a friend who is the sole hero on earth and equal to a god is, for those who bear the burden of the earth, generally dependent upon some purpose. And what kind of purpose could there possibly be, were it proposed, that would bring Your Majesty into a state of friendship?"
For wealth is but an external appendage for a king who desires to accumulate glory;
and when he rests upon his two arms alone, even the other limbs have no opportunity to fulfill their desire to provide assistance, let alone external people.
What satisfaction could there be in the proposal of giving away a mere portion of the earth to one who devours entire villages from the four oceans?
Even the lure of bestowing a beautiful maiden is of no avail for one whose gaze has become spoiled by the sight of the lotus-face of Lakṣmī.
Thus, since all possible means have failed to achieve this objective, let Your Majesty hear me as I rely solely upon a mere request.
For the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa is like a single tawny-eyed elephant [in battle] against the enemy of Anahga (Kāma), who is accompanied by Your Majesty.
Like Daśaratha with Gotrabhid, like Dhanañjaya with Puṣkarākṣa,
and like Vakra with Duryodhana.
Like the Malaya breeze with the month of Mādhava,
he desires an ageless union;
and if Your Majesty’s heart is likewise inclined toward friendship, know that they will perform their service even while disguised under another pretext.

"Since you are our friends, why do you remain thus? Let it be commanded that the Lord of Kāmarūpa may enjoy a firm embrace from the King—his bracelets jingling as the jeweled fragments of his armlets are struck by the tips of Viṣṇu’s massive armlets, like Mount Mandara against the god.
Let the Fortune of Prāgjyotiṣa at last caress her eyes for a long time upon this moon-like face, which is a river of nectar consisting of inexhaustible, pure beauty and grace."
"If Your Majesty does not accept this request, then, O Lord, what am I to say?

When he had ceased speaking, the King— already filled with great respect for the prince due to his previously known noble qualities, and now having that affection raised to its highest pitch by the news of the prince's attainment of the imperial canopy— spoke with reverence as if feeling somewhat abashed.
He said: "Haṃsavega!

How could the mind of one such as I ever turn otherwise—even in a dream—toward such a great soul, of noble lineage, a mass of merit, the foremost among the virtuous, and a friend from afar? Even the rays of the sun, though capable of scorching the entire world, become cool when they fall upon a lotus-pond that brings joy to the eyes of the three worlds. And as for us, bought by his manifold virtues, who are we to speak of friendship?"
The ten directions have become the handmaidens of the sweetness of the virtuous.
For the sake of the night-lotus, whose likeness is produced by its nature being exclusively pure and radiant, who has ever declared that the cool-rayed moon was its servant?
And the prince’s resolve is auspicious; he himself is strong-armed, and when his friend has taken up the bow, whom else would he pay homage to, other than Hara?
"My affection has been nourished by this resolve. Even toward a haughty beast such as a lion, there is great respect in my heart; how much more so toward a friend?
Therefore, I shall strive in such a way that this longing to see the prince does not cause us distress for long."
Haṃsavega, however, made this representation: “O Lord, what more can distress your noble self now? You have already spoken enough.
For the virtuous are indeed afraid of servitude.”
Even therein, this lineage of Vaiṣṇavas is preeminently rich in self-respect;
let alone our own master’s lineage.
Let Your Majesty observe how a man, when being driven toward service by either extreme old age or dire misfortune—as if by a wicked woman—is compelled to act.
Of one being impelled by a wife or by an insatiable craving; of one being agitated by various desires born of youth or by false resolves like wayward children;
and of one beholding a very advanced state of life, like an old maiden fit only for seeking another's hand.

He was being assailed by an attack from all the planets as if they were ill-disposed kinsmen in his own house; he was being pursued by past actions as if by foul servants who are difficult to cast off; he felt as if he were about to enter the royal palace—which causes a burning heat throughout the entire body like a fire of dried cow-dung for a sinner—with all his sensory powers impaired, yet still falsely harboring a longing to seize the multitude of sense-objects within his heart.
At the very outset, at the foot of the archway, he was like a withering garland of young shoots held back by door-keepers;
as he entered the gate, he was oppressed and struck by others like a deer;
and he was repeatedly repelled by the blows of the hands of the circle of ushers, like the leather bag used for elephant-dung.
Like a sprout from a treasure-tree turning downward out of a longing for wealth, like one who, though not seeking it at all, falls into agitation when cast far away by being flung open and released,
and like one who, though thornless, is seized and hurled with great force as soon as he has touched the soles of the feet.
He was like the god of love, burnt by the glance of Śiva who was provoked by his untimely approach;
yet, though he was threatened by the wrath of one approaching his destruction, his facial color remained unchanged like that of a monkey.
He was like a Brahmin ascetic, whose skull is rubbed daily by the prostrations of salutation.
For one devoid of sensory contact, performing impure deeds,
fallen from both worlds like Triśaṅku, remaining with head downward day and night,
and making himself easy to carry like a horse by means of fodder;
Like one who lies fasting and has resolved to give up his life,
he wasted away his body; like a dog turned away from its own mate,
he struck at his own honor which clung to him through base actions.

Like a funeral rice-ball offered on ground unsuitable for a hungry ghost, his life was lived in vain, its vitality consumed by the greed of the tongue like that of a crow; he approached the king’s favorites as if they were trees in a cremation ground, their bark made harsh by the ashes of a fire demon; and he was surrounded by the chatter of royal parrots, whose sweetness was produced only by perverted tongues and whose passion was revealed merely upon their beaks.
Like a child being enticed by toys, he did nothing that was not performed; like a vetāla possessed by the power of a king, he was subject to no restraint;
like Citradhanus, he was ever-bowed in the single act of falsely attributing qualities to himself; and his splendor had been extinguished.
Like a heap of refuse that carries away discarded offerings, gathering dust with a broom;
like one suffering from a phlegmatic disorder who is daily provoked by pungent substances;
or like a follower of the Sugata who, having conceived a world-weariness born of the realization that all things are empty of intrinsic meaning, longs for the saffron robes.
Even at night, he was like an offering of food for the Mothers being scattered in all directions;
like one fallen into impurity, his course of suffering was intensified by lying upon a bed of kusha grass;
and like a balance-beam, he had cast aside his dignity and bent even to fetch water.
Of one who is excessively miserly, who is dissatisfied even with bowing his head alone and yet touches [another's] feet even with his words;
who has been abandoned by shame as if terrified by the blows of the cane from a merciless staff-bearer;
and who has been forsaken by self-respect as if its scope had been snatched away by a heart shrunken through wretchedness.

Of one who is bereft of dignity—as if by that very dignity being incensed at the acceptance of despicable deeds; of a fool who, through faith in wealth, accumulates afflictions, and by the desire for his own advancement, increases his own humiliation;
who, despite the forest fragrant with the scent of various flowers, stretches out his cupped hands in thirst.
Though he was a son of noble family, he approached him like one who had committed an offense, trembling with fear;
though he was handsome, his birth was as fruitless as that of a flower in a painting;
and though he was learned, his mouth uttered errors like that of a fool.
Though possessing power, he was like a leper with his two hands shriveled;
he was roasted without fire during times of equal or superior prosperity,
and suffocated to death during times of being leveled with the lowly.
Of one who has been treated as a blade of grass by insults, who burns with the wind of suffering without relief, and who,
though devoted, is treated as if undevoted.
Though devoid of heat, it causes torment to its kinsmen;
though a celestial mansion, it is without movement;
and though its dignity has vanished, it descends below.

Even though he was devoid of a living being, he sold human flesh; even though he was free from intoxication, his conduct was uncontrolled; and even though he was not a yogin, his self was brought under the power of meditation.
Of this scorched-headed man who bows upon rising from bed,
who mocks the lineage of others while dancing day and night to make the wise laugh,
and who is a firebrand to his family, burning down his own kin.
What atonement can there be for a human beast who bows his neck even when receiving a mere blade of grass;
for a lump of flesh born solely for the purpose of filling a belly, a disease to its mother;
and for a hireling who performs unmeritorious deeds?
What is the practice to be performed? For one who has gone where is there peace? What is the nature of life?
What is this pride of manhood? What are these so-called pleasures? And what is this craving for enjoyment?

The dreadful word "slave" drags everything downward like thick mud; fie on that breath of life! Let wealth go to its destruction, let there be no birth for that which has no existence—salutations to those divine pleasures! Here is my joined palms to sovereignty;

let that Goddess Śrī remain far away. May he, the ascetic capable of bestowing grace upon those free from curses, bring welfare to her along with her retinue—for whose sake he shall offer his head as an oblation to the cows.

A eunuch devoted to the pleasures of the mouth, a worm consisting of putrid flesh beyond counting, a hell on earth; with his head greyed by the dust of others' feet, he is a walking footstool; a male cuckoo in his plaintive warbling, and a peacock in his harsh, screeching cries.
The large tortoise in its rubbing against the chest; the dog in its making of base flatteries;
the chameleon in its mockery of the head.
The mongoose in self-concealments,
the bamboo in musical modulations,
and the body of a courtesan in the pain of assuming various postures.
He was straw among beings who were like rice-grains;
he was a foot-massager among those who provide such service; and he was a ball among those who strike with the palms of their hands.
A lute-neck is [but wood] struck by a plectrum;
even a wretched servant among mortals is like a royal cobra,
or even a mere grain of broken rice is like a fine *kalama* rice stalk.
"Better for a high-minded man even a moment of honor than the enjoyment of sovereignty over the three worlds for a hundred years.
Therefore, let Your Majesty take to heart that His Highness the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, having been thus welcomed by us, will arrive in just a few days. Having said this, he became silent;
after a long time, he bowed and departed.
The king also spent that night with his heart seized by the longing to see the prince;
for the self-surrender of the great is a spell of subjugation that requires no root-mantra.
And at dawn, having given a profuse array of gifts entrusted to a chief envoy, he dispatched Haṃsavega.
From that time forward, he himself set out toward the enemy with incessant marches.

However, one day, he heard from a messenger that Bhaṇḍi had arrived and was encamped nearby, having brought with him the entire army of the Mālava king, acquired through the strength of Rājyavardhana’s arm.
Upon hearing this, the fire of grief for his brother flared up anew; his heart became terrified at the prospect of seeing him, as if shrouded in the darkness of a swoon.

Having abandoned all his activities, he entered his own palace and remained there for a moment with his royal retinue, awaiting his arrival, while the attendants stood silent and motionless as they were barred by the doorkeeper.

Then Bhaṇḍi appeared on a single horse, surrounded by a few young men of noble family, dressed in soiled garments, and with a heart filled with the darts of his enemies' arrows— a heart protected from bursting by a framework of many iron spikes driven into it.

With his beard clinging to his heart as if it were honored by his master, he manifested his grief; his ornaments consisted only of the auspicious bracelets swinging from his long arms, which had grown flaccid from the cessation of exercise; and with his lower lip—its color faded from the careless consumption of betel and drying from the force of long sighs emitted as it was scorched by the fire of sorrow—he appeared as if ashamed for the offense of having maintained his life despite being separated from his master.
With his face veiled as if by a cloth by the mass of his tears,
appearing to enter his own body with limbs weakened by shame, and as if vomiting the heat of his arms through long sighs that had become feeble,
he was like a sinner.
As if guilty, as if treacherous, as if robbed;
Like one who has been led astray, like a lord of the herd dejected by the fall of his leader, like a swift-footed elephant restrained by a goad,
or like a lotus pond robbed of its splendor at the setting of the sun.
Dejected as if by the death of Duryodhana,
like the ocean deprived of its jewels, the son of Droṇa approached the palace gate;
having dismounted from his horse, he entered the royal residence with his face cast down.
Even from afar, having ceased his cries, he fell at [the king's] feet.
The lord of the earth, seeing him, rose and went forward with short steps; lifting him up and embracing him firmly around the neck, he wept piteously for a very long time.
When the intensity of his grief had subsided, he returned as before and sat down upon his own throne.
When Bhaṇḍi had first washed his face, he washed his own face as well;
and after some portion of time had passed, he asked about the news of his brother's death.
Then Bhaṇḍi related the entire account exactly as it had occurred.
Then the king said to him, "What is this matter concerning Rājyaśrī?
He replied again, "Your Majesty,
when Prince Rājyavardhana had passed away and Guptanāman was taken prisoner, Queen Rājyaśrī escaped from her confinement at Kuśasthala and entered the Vindhya forest with her attendants."
"I have heard news from the world:
many searchers have been dispatched for her, yet they have not returned even now.
Upon hearing this, the king said, "What is the use of other trackers? Abandoning all other duties, I myself shall go wherever she is."
"You too, taking up your army, set out toward Gauḍa.
Having said this, he rose and went to the bathing area.
Then, having had his grief-induced beard shaved and having bathed in the quarters of the chief chamberlain, [he returned].

Having manifested his favor by sending bodily garments, flowers, unguents, and ornaments, he dined together with Bhaṇḍi and spent the day in his company. Then, on the following day, Bhaṇḍi approached the king like a servant and informed him: "May Your Majesty behold the army and its equipment belonging to the King of Mālava, acquired through the strength of the arm of the illustrious Rājyavardhana."
Thus addressed, the king, having granted permission with the words, "Let it be done so," caused [them] to be displayed. Namely:
[elephants] whose temples were muddied by the masses of bees buzzing with the fragrance of rut-wine flowing incessantly;
Like moving boulders from mountain slopes,
like clouds descended upon the earth with deep thundering roars, emitting the fragrance of blossoming *saptacchada* groves,
they appeared like autumn days gathered into a single mass.
He saw elephants numbering in the thousands;
horses with the speed of deer, enchanting with circles of beautiful yak-tail whisks adorned with lovely gold;
and various ornaments that, by emitting rays like a shower of morning sunlight, turned the ten directions into a single rainbow.

He brought forth pearl necklaces that caused wonder, which were as delicate as the fragrance of the breasts of Mālava women maddened by love, and which, though their stars were washed over by the flood of his own moonlight,
served as white fly-whisks— pure as the mass of rays from the moon’s feet and like his own fame—
and a white parasol made of gold, its handle like the lotus that is the abode of Śrī.
He saw courtesans who had descended [to earth] out of passion for the daring pleasures of many battles like celestial nymphs;
the regalia of sovereignty, such as thrones, couches, and seats;
and the entire circle of Mālava kings, their pairs of feet rendered motionless by shackles of black iron.
Then, having examined all of it— including the complete inventories with their written records and the jars of the treasury adorned with ornamental crests—

the protector of the earth commanded his superintendents to take possession of it according to their respective jurisdictions. On another day, he set out on horseback alone to search for his sister and reached the Vindhya forest.
After traveling for only a limited number of stages,

he then entered [the village], which from afar was being turned grey by the smoke of wild grain seed-vessels whose fires were spreading through the scattering of burning sixty-day-old chaff; [the village] where massive banyan trees were encircled by cow-pens constructed from heaps of dry branches, and where cowherds— possessed by rage because their calves had been killed— were muttering frantic incantations.

The forest regions were characterized by axes belonging to wood-gatherers from neighboring villages who were being forcibly carried away by unrestrained forest guards; by groves of dense trees where shrines to Cāmuṇḍā had been constructed;

and by weak farmers, distressed by the burden of supporting their families due to the region’s predominantly wild nature, who practiced agriculture primarily with spades and were parched by the heat of the highlands.
The fields were broken into small fragments of threshing floors for abundant rice, with little space left between them; they were as hard as black clay, appearing as if made of iron,
with thick sprouts of thorny shrubs rising from trunks planted here and there, and were overgrown with difficult-to-traverse *śyāmāka* weeds and abounding in *alambuṣa* plants.

It was a region where the fields were sparse and interspersed with scattered groves of *kokilākṣa* shrubs; where, because the land was only barely tilled due to the difficulty of cultivation, the soil was not yet worn by excessive coming and going; and which indicated the presence of wild beasts by the high platforms erected near the outskirts of the fields.
And in every direction, the shade of the trees along the roadside was marked by fresh sprouts, grey with the dust from the travelers' feet rubbing against them.
[The hermitage] had small huts constructed from seamless bamboo mats, situated near newly dug wells adorned with clusters of *sāla* flowers easily found in the forest;
these huts were occupied by rows of shallow bowls filled with parched grain and entwined by the curly antennae of insects,
while their immediate grounds were variegated with the stones of *jambu* fruits chewed by travelers.
Their hair stood on end like clusters of kadamba blossoms covered in rising dust;
their thirst was quenched by wooden stools occupied by rows of water-jars with bristling necks;
and their fatigue was relieved by jars cooled by the moisture of the sandy ground.

The coolness of the water was being produced in the jars, which were darkened by moss clinging to them; the quarters of the sky were cooled by fragments of pale-red sugar-candy drawn from water-jars; and there were clusters of pale-red flowers tied in garlands at the mouths of the pots.

It was a place where the sacrificial posts (*sthāṇu*) were thick with clusters of unripe mango fruits—fresh and succulent yet drying on stalks, tended by rows of leaf-bundles whose sprouts were bristling with spray;

where the water at the roadside wells for entering the forest was being drunk by successions of resting bands of wandering mendicants (*kārpaṭika*); which seemed to drive away the summer heat by its coolness in one spot, while elsewhere it seemed to make it take hold through the fires burning the wood gathered for charcoal; and which was everywhere covered with provisions for the journey, deposited in the houses of neighboring villages by elderly men maintained by householders.

With limbs marked by the exertion of felling formidable timber, with heavy axes resting upon their shoulders and necks from which hung bundles of morning provisions, clad in rags as a penance for the sin of thievery, and with their necks bound by triple coils of black cane vines tied in knots, their mouths covered by leaf-pipes;

There were forest-dwellers entering the woods to gather firewood with water-carrying baskets on their heads, leading pairs of powerful oxen before them; there were hunters wandering outside with snares and traps set thickly for the purpose of piercing wild beasts, holding circles of nets made from deer-sinews and loops of hair; and there were fowlers carrying cages of partridges, quails, francolins, and other birds, with young birds hanging from cords tied to their shoulders and nets suspended from their arms.

[The place was filled] with wandering young hunters playing at the chase of fluttering birds, their hands eager for the slaps of those addicted to the long hair of women whose bracelets had slipped off; with young gamblers roaming about, coaxing packs of dogs that were as restless as partridges hidden within clumps of grass;
and with bundles of bark garments fit for the drinking of *śīdhu* liquor, possessing a hue as astringent as the throats of full-grown ruddy geese.
He brought countless sacks of *dhātakī* flowers recently gathered, still radiant with their mineral-like luster; abundant bundles of soft cotton, *atasī* seeds, and *gaṇapaṭṭa* fibers;
loads of honey from bees; and heaps of wax-beeswax in the form of unblemished circular discs; loads of *lāmajjaka* grass and tufts of *muñja* reeds;
barkless *khadira* wood; and many loads of *kuṣṭha* and of *rodhra* trees, which were tawny like the thick manes of wild lions.

The horizon was filled on all sides by country women hurrying toward the nearby village, their heads laden with baskets brimming with various forest fruits gathered from the woods, their minds preoccupied with thoughts of selling them;

and by the arrivals of long lines of carts, drawn by bulls and bullocks that were bellowing in anger as they were driven along, their backs grey with dust, scattering the old earth and heaps of dried cow-dung, and rattling with the creaking of their playfully moving wheels.

And [the region was characterized] by bamboo fences that were easily leaped over by deer playfully springing up as they were startled by the sticks wielded by tame drivers who had been driven away by the cultivation of the parched and barren fields being prepared; by tall bamboo shoots snapped by hares fearing the bleached white skeletons of cows; by sugarcane groves whose wide, thick stalks were being diligently tended; and by dense thickets of bamboo branches suitable for making bows.

with garden enclosures difficult to enter due to rows of thorny *karañja* trees; with courtyards dense with thickets of castor-oil plants, *vacā*, *avaṅgaka*, *surasā*, *sūraṇa*, drumsticks, *granthiparṇa*, wild millet, and *garmud* beans; and providing shade through the spreading vines of yams planted on high wooden posts driven into the ground.
[The place was] filled with calves tied to stakes of *khadira* wood driven into the ground beneath circular *badarī* bower-circles;

its layout could only be inferred by the crowing of cocks; it contained small pools for birds fashioned from the bases of *nāga-stambha* pillars; it was strewn with clusters of pale-red *badara* fruits;
and its walls were constructed from fences made of reeds, bamboo, and split *nalaka* stalks.
With heaps of charcoal bound with *balvaja* grass in pavilions marked by circles drawn with *kiṃśuka* flowers and yellow pigment (*gorocanā*); abounding in accumulations of *śālmalī* fruit-wool;
and containing nearby pieces of reeds, rice, lotus roots, white water-lily seeds, and bamboo-grain.

It was filled with the finest *ālābū* seeds; it possessed mats woven from heaps of *kāśmarya* shrubs, soiled with ash and withered; it abounded in dried *rājādana* and *madana* fruits; it was full of *madhūka* liquor and wine;
and it was never without jars, pots, baskets, and granaries containing *rājamāṣa*, *trapuṣa*, *karkaṭikā*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, and *ālābu* seeds.
He beheld a forest village provided with the dwellings of forest-dwellers, which included reared wild cats, *māludhāna* snakes, mongooses, and various kinds of grain;
and there he passed that very day.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Acquisition of the Umbrella," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by the illustrious great poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
